archetypes.name: Axial-mode helix
archetypes.summary: End-fire helix radiating circular polarisation along its axis.

synthesis.notes: a ground plane of at least 0.75 lambda diameter; smaller plates raise the back lobe

analysis.notes: The classic Kraus formula, kept because it is the one everyone quotes - and now measured rather than merely suspected. Against a full-wave solve its error grows with BOTH length and circumference. At C = lambda and 13 degrees it is 1.6 dB high at 3 turns, 2.8 at 5, 3.8 at 10 and 4.4 at 20; across the whole design core (C/lambda 0.9 to 1.1, pitch 12 to 14 degrees) it is 0.9 to 5.4 dB high from five turns up. It is roughly right only in the short, small corner - 3 turns at C/lambda = 0.9. This is the progressive divergence this spec's note always claimed, now with a size on it. It goes further wrong at the band edges: up to 8.7 dB high at C/lambda = 1.2 on a long helix, where the axial mode collapses but C^3 keeps climbing, and slightly LOW at C/lambda = 0.8 with few turns. Use gain_dbi.

Solved, not assumed. Fitted over the design core only - C/lambda 0.9 to 1.1, N 3 to 20, pitch 12 to 14 degrees - where the surface is smooth; worst fit error 0.35 dB. Outside that the gain has a cliff a polynomial cannot follow, so the full grid is in this spec's tables instead. Directivity equals gain here: the conductor is lossless. Note the pitch dependence runs the OPPOSITE way to Kraus: steeper pitch lengthens the helix and Kraus rises, but it moves the phase velocity off the end-fire optimum and the real gain falls, about 0.5 dB per degree. Method of moments on the helix over an infinite PEC ground plane by image theory (otahub.num.mom.helix_over_ground), wire radius 0.005 lambda. Checked by a second computational path - directivity by reciprocity from the open-circuit voltage under plane-wave illumination, which never touches the pattern integral - agreeing to 0.02 dB at N = 10; power balance holds to 1e-4 and the image structure's far field is mirror-symmetric to 1e-7. NaN outside the core (C/lambda 1.2 read 16.3 dBi where the solved table has 11.8); the tables carry the rest.
Kraus: 52/(C/lambda * sqrt(N*S/lambda)). Too narrow by the same token that his gain is too high - 34 degrees for the canonical helix where the solver finds 46.

Half-power beamwidth in a plane through the axis, solved. Design core only; worst fit error 6.0%. Method of moments on the helix over an infinite PEC ground plane by image theory (otahub.num.mom.helix_over_ground), wire radius 0.005 lambda. Checked by a second computational path - directivity by reciprocity from the open-circuit voltage under plane-wave illumination, which never touches the pattern integral - agreeing to 0.02 dB at N = 10; power balance holds to 1e-4 and the image structure's far field is mirror-symmetric to 1e-7.

AR = (2N+1)/(2N): the Hansen-Woodyard ideal, and a lower bound rather than a prediction. An untapered helix solved here shows 1.01 to 1.24 on axis for N >= 6 in the design core, varying irregularly with the standing wave off the open end - too irregular to fit honestly, which is why real helices taper the last turn.

INDICATIVE: Kraus's Rin ~ 140*(C/lambda). It describes one feed, not the helix. The solver shows the helix body barely cares how it is fed - gain moves 0.1 dB between feed heights of 0.01 and 0.05 lambda - but the terminal impedance swings from about 70 to 150 ohm over that range and from 40 to 180 ohm across wire gauges, with -50 to -90 ohm of reactance. Matching is set by the feed geometry, which this spec does not describe.

validity: axial mode requires 0.75 < C/lambda < 1.33; outside this the helix reverts to normal mode or breaks into higher-order radiation

gain_dbi and hpbw_deg are fitted over the design core C/lambda 0.9 to 1.1, N 3 to 20, pitch 12 to 14 degrees; the tables field carries the solved values out to 0.8 and 1.2, where long helices lose several dB

solved for a wire radius of 0.005 lambda on an infinite ground plane. Wire size genuinely matters: 0.002 lambda reads about 1 dB lower and 0.01 about 0.8 dB higher at N = 10, by shifting the phase velocity
mesh: 16 segments per turn sits about 0.15 dB below the converged value
input resistance and axial ratio remain indicative: both are governed by feed and end details this spec does not describe
N >= 3 for a well-formed end-fire beam

known_cases.source: Canonical Kraus helix: C = lambda, 10 turns, 13.3 deg pitch gives S = 0.236 lambda, G = 11.8 + 10*log10(1*10*0.236) = 15.53 dBi, HPBW = 52/sqrt(2.36) = 33.85 deg, AR = 21/20, Rin = 140 ohm. Kraus, Antennas 2nd ed., Ch. 7
C = lambda = 299.79 mm at 1 GHz, so D = C/pi = 95.44 mm. Kraus, Antennas 2nd ed., Ch. 7

Method of moments, 10 turns, C = 1.0 lambda, 13 degrees: 11.62 dBi and a 46.2 degree beam. Kraus's formula gives 15.43 dBi, +3.8 dB off; the 'corrected' formula this spec used to recommend for design gave 17.95 dBi, +6.3 dB off.

Method of moments, 6 turns, C = 0.9 lambda, 12 degrees: 10.33 dBi and a 61.3 degree beam. Kraus's formula gives 11.48 dBi, +1.2 dB off; the 'corrected' formula this spec used to recommend for design gave 12.07 dBi, +1.7 dB off.

Method of moments, 15 turns, C = 1.1 lambda, 14 degrees: 13.65 dBi and a 30.0 degree beam. Kraus's formula gives 18.77 dBi, +5.1 dB off; the 'corrected' formula this spec used to recommend for design gave 23.23 dBi, +9.6 dB off.

Method of moments, 20 turns, C = 1.0 lambda, 13 degrees: 14.04 dBi and a 30.5 degree beam. Kraus's formula gives 18.44 dBi, +4.4 dB off; the 'corrected' formula this spec used to recommend for design gave 24.49 dBi, +10.4 dB off.

references: Kraus, Antennas 2nd ed., Ch. 7
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 10 (10.3)
King & Wong, Characteristics of 1 to 8 wavelength uniform helical antennas, IEEE Trans. AP-28, 1980
Gain and beamwidth solved here by method of moments over an infinite ground plane by image theory, cross-checked by receive-mode reciprocity

mom_gain.source: Method of moments, otahub.num.mom.helix_over_ground, wire radius 0.005 lambda, infinite PEC ground, 16 segments per turn
mom_gain.note: The whole grid, including the band edges the fitted metrics leave out. Read the C/lambda = 1.2 column for long helices: gain falls several dB as the axial mode gives out, which no formula here reproduces.

archetypes.name: Normal-mode helix
archetypes.summary: Electrically small helix radiating broadside to its axis; the rubber-duck antenna.

analysis.notes: AR = 2*S*lambda/C^2. AR = 1 (circular polarisation) requires C^2 = 2*S*lambda; AR >> 1 means the helix behaves as a short dipole, AR << 1 as a small loop.
the turn spacing that would give AR = 1 for this diameter
must stay well below 0.75 to remain in normal mode
the pattern is that of a short dipole or small loop, so D = 1.5 (1.76 dBi)

validity: normal mode requires the whole helix to be electrically small: N*S << lambda and C << lambda
efficiency is usually poor and dominated by conductor loss, which is not modelled
a real rubber-duck is detuned substantially by the hand and body holding it

known_cases.source: D = 10 mm, S = 2 mm at 1 GHz: C = 31.42 mm, AR = 2*S*lambda/C^2 = 1.215. Above unity, so this helix is mildly dipole-dominant; AR = 1 would need S = 1.646 mm. Equivalently AR = S/(C^2/(2*lambda)) = 2.0/1.646. Kraus, Antennas 2nd ed., Ch. 7
C^2/(2*lambda) = 1.646 mm would give AR = 1 at this diameter. Kraus, Antennas 2nd ed., Ch. 7

references: Kraus, Antennas 2nd ed., Ch. 7
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 10 (10.3.1)

archetypes.name: Log-periodic dipole array
archetypes.summary: Frequency-independent array of scaled dipoles; constant gain over a decade or more.

parameters.name: feeder characteristic impedance
parameters.description: the transposed line joining the elements; it sets the input impedance

parameters.name: element length-to-diameter ratio
parameters.description: held constant along the array so the structure is truly log-periodic

synthesis.notes: Carrel's optimum relative spacing for a given tau
Inverts sigma = (1-tau)/(4*tan(alpha)), which is the defining LPDA geometry relation
longest element is a half wave at the lowest frequency
The 1.3 factor extends the structure past the top of the band so the active region is fully formed there (the bandwidth of the active region, Bar). Without it the gain droops badly at the high end.

analysis.notes: Bs = B * Bar, the structure bandwidth actually built

Linear reading of the Carrel directivity chart along the optimum-sigma line, 0.8 < tau < 0.95. It HOLDS: against the full-wave log-period mean it is within 0.6 dB at every tau, -0.55 to +0.57 dB. What a single number hides is the periodic ripple - the directivity repeats with period tau in frequency and swings 2.0 dB peak-to-peak at tau = 0.8, 0.7 at 0.9 and 0.2 at 0.95; the tables field carries the solved mean, minimum and maximum. Checked against a full-wave solve: method of moments on every element with the feeder as a transmission-line network (otahub.num.mom.lpda_model, solve_network), averaged over one full log-period in frequency with the active region held seven elements from the back and twelve from the front. The feeder coupling is itself checked three ways, including power conservation through the lossless feeder to 1e-4.
from the apex geometry: the boom spans the two extreme element half-lengths
Average characteristic impedance of a dipole of the given length-to-diameter ratio, the element term in the design relation.
Mean spacing factor, sigma' = sigma/sqrt(tau).

R = Z0/sqrt(1 + Z0/(4 sigma' Za)), the standard design relation, and the metric this spec was missing entirely: choosing the feeder is how an LPDA is matched. Against the full-wave solve it is -6% to +11% over feeders of 50 to 200 ohm and element ratios of 60 to 250, reading a few percent low except on the stiffest 50 ohm feeder. The solved input is nearly real: reactance stays within 18 ohm across a period, a small fraction of the resistance. Checked against a full-wave solve: method of moments on every element with the feeder as a transmission-line network (otahub.num.mom.lpda_model, solve_network), averaged over one full log-period in frequency with the active region held seven elements from the back and twelve from the front. The feeder coupling is itself checked three ways, including power conservation through the lossless feeder to 1e-4.
The same relation solved for the feeder that gives a 50 ohm input.

validity: 0.8 < tau < 0.95; below 0.8 the gain collapses, above 0.95 the array grows impractically long for marginal gain
assumes optimum sigma; a design off that line has lower directivity than the chart value
directivity is a log-period mean; the real antenna ripples about it by up to 2 dB peak-to-peak at tau = 0.8, far less at high tau
the tau = 0.95 value is the least converged: a high-tau array has a wide active region, and enlarging the solved structure moved it 0.6 dB

requires the feeder to be transposed between adjacent elements. Without the reversal the array does NOT reliably fire backwards, as this spec used to say: it loses its front-to-back ratio altogether - within a few dB either way - and its input impedance swings tenfold inside one period. It stops being frequency-independent, which is the point of the design
input resistance depends on the feeder and element thickness; the design relation is within about 10% of a full-wave solve

known_cases.source: tau = 0.9: sigma_opt = 0.243*0.9 - 0.051 = 0.1677, alpha = arctan(0.1/(4*0.1677)) = 8.48 deg. Longest element = lambda/2 at 100 MHz = 1.499 m. Carrel, The Design of Log-Periodic Dipole Antennas, IRE Int. Conv. Rec., 1961
A decade of bandwidth with the 1.3 active-region allowance needs 1 + ceil(ln(13)/ln(1/0.9)) = 26 elements.

R = Z0/sqrt(1 + Z0/(4 sigma' Za)) with sigma' = 0.1677/sqrt(0.9) and Za = 120(ln 125 - 2.25) = 309.4 ohm gives 82.8 ohm on a 100 ohm feeder. The full-wave solve, averaged over a log-period, gives 85.9 ohm. Inverting the same relation, a 50 ohm input needs a 56.0 ohm feeder.

R = Z0/sqrt(1 + Z0/(4 sigma' Za)) with sigma' = 0.1677/sqrt(0.9) and Za = 120(ln 125 - 2.25) = 309.4 ohm gives 45.1 ohm on a 50 ohm feeder. The full-wave solve, averaged over a log-period, gives 40.6 ohm. Inverting the same relation, a 50 ohm input needs a 56.0 ohm feeder.

references: Carrel, The Design of Log-Periodic Dipole Antennas, IRE Int. Conv. Rec., 1961
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 10 (11.5)
Directivity, its periodic ripple and the input resistance checked here by method of moments with the feeder modelled as a transposed transmission line

mom_directivity.source: Method of moments with a transposed 100 ohm feeder, L/d = 125, one full log-period sampled at six frequencies
mom_directivity.note: The ripple is the part the fitted directivity cannot show.

archetypes.name: Yagi-Uda array
archetypes.summary: Driven dipole with one reflector and several parasitic directors; the classic TV antenna.

synthesis.notes: NBS optimised designs place the reflector at about 0.482 lambda
driven element runs 0.45-0.49 lambda depending on the matching arrangement; a folded dipole is usual, to lift the 20-30 ohm parasitic-loaded impedance toward 300 ohm

analysis.notes: SOLVED: the six optimised NBS designs (Viezbicke, NBS Technical Note 688 - reflector 0.2 lambda behind the driven element, the tabulated director lengths and spacings, element diameter 0.0085 lambda) built and solved in free space, lossless, by two independent methods - the thin-wire method of moments (otahub.num.mom, taken to zero segment length) and coupled Hallen equations with point matching - which agree within 0.08 dB: 8.93, 11.21, 12.39, 14.23, 15.37 and 16.10 dBi for booms of 0.4 to 4.2 wavelengths. Fitted in log10(boom), 0.085 dB worst. This spec fitted NBS's tabulated 7.1 to 14.2 dB and called them dBi; NBS quotes gain over a half-wave dipole, so it read 1.9-2.1 dB low. Read as dBd, NBS's measured figures sit 0.04 dB below to 0.32 dB above the solved ones. Valid only for designs on that optimised curve - an arbitrary Yagi of the same boom does worse.
The same over a half-wave dipole (2.15 dBi), the unit NBS tabulated in.

INDICATIVE, not derived: optimised NBS designs aim at roughly 20 dB. The ratio is positive (the spec had -20). Both solvers put it anywhere from 13 to 27 dB across the six designs and neither is converged in it - the back lobe is a near-cancellation, sensitive to the driven element's length and the mesh - so no figure is derived here.

SOLVED: E-plane (the plane of the elements and the boom) half-power beamwidth of the same six solved designs, fitted as a power of the boom: 1.7% worst. 60 degrees at 0.4 wavelengths, 28.6 at 4.2. The 55/sqrt(boom) this spec carried was 27-45% too wide on short booms (87 degrees at 0.4).
SOLVED the same way: H-plane half-power beamwidth, 2.9% worst on the six designs; wider than the E plane, 89.5 degrees at 0.4 wavelengths and 30.2 at 4.2.

The NBS designs' director counts: 1, 3, 4, 10, 15 and 13 at booms of 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 2.2, 3.2 and 4.2 wavelengths (their spacing is 0.2 lambda except 0.25 at 1.2 and 0.308 at 4.2), interpolated between. The round(3 x boom) this spec used missed three of the six. Use the NBS tables for an actual build.

validity: gain fit is valid only along the NBS optimised curve, for boom 0.4 to 4.2 lambda
element lengths and spacings must come from the NBS tables (see the tables field); the fit gives the achievable gain, not a recipe
gain saturates: doubling the boom past about 4 lambda buys under 1 dB
input impedance is low (20-30 ohm) and strongly dependent on director spacing; not modelled here
F/B and beamwidth entries are indicative, not derived
gain and beamwidths are for the NBS optimised designs at element diameter 0.0085 lambda, solved in free space and lossless; front-to-back is indicative

nbs_optimised.source: Viezbicke, Yagi Antenna Design, NBS Technical Note 688, 1976
nbs_optimised.note: Viezbicke's optimised designs. Director spacings and lengths vary along the boom; consult the source for the per-element dimensions.

known_cases.source: NBS tabulated 10.20 dB over a half-wave dipole for a 1.2-wavelength boom (Viezbicke, NBS Technical Note 688) - 12.35 dBi. That design built and solved (otahub.num.mom, taken to zero segment length): 12.386 dBi; coupled Hallen equations give 12.434. The fit is checked against the solve, not against NBS.

NBS tabulated 14.20 dB over a half-wave dipole for a 4.2-wavelength boom (Viezbicke, NBS Technical Note 688) - 16.35 dBi. That design built and solved (otahub.num.mom, taken to zero segment length): 16.099 dBi; coupled Hallen equations give 16.102. The fit is checked against the solve, not against NBS.

NBS tabulated 7.10 dB over a half-wave dipole for a 0.4-wavelength boom (Viezbicke, NBS Technical Note 688) - 9.25 dBi. That design built and solved (otahub.num.mom, taken to zero segment length): 8.927 dBi; coupled Hallen equations give 9.005. The fit is checked against the solve, not against NBS.
NBS 0.8-wavelength design (3 directors) solved in free space: 11.209 dBi by the method of moments, 11.230 by coupled Hallen equations; NBS tabulated 9.20 dB over a half-wave dipole.
NBS 2.2-wavelength design (10 directors) solved in free space: 14.228 dBi by the method of moments, 14.223 by coupled Hallen equations; NBS tabulated 12.25 dB over a half-wave dipole.
NBS 3.2-wavelength design (15 directors) solved in free space: 15.370 dBi by the method of moments, 15.336 by coupled Hallen equations; NBS tabulated 13.40 dB over a half-wave dipole.
Half-power widths of the solved NBS 0.4-wavelength design (method of moments, E plane through the elements and boom, H plane across them), read off its pattern: 60.1 and 89.5 degrees.
The NBS table's director count for this boom: 1.
Half-power widths of the solved NBS 1.2-wavelength design (method of moments, E plane through the elements and boom, H plane across them), read off its pattern: 42.5 and 48.9 degrees.
The NBS table's director count for this boom: 4.
Half-power widths of the solved NBS 4.2-wavelength design (method of moments, E plane through the elements and boom, H plane across them), read off its pattern: 28.6 and 30.2 degrees.
The NBS table's director count for this boom: 13.

references: Viezbicke, Yagi Antenna Design, NBS Technical Note 688, 1976
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 10 (10.3.3)

archetypes.name: Terminated travelling-wave long wire
archetypes.summary: Straight wire carrying a single travelling wave into a matched termination; radiates in a cone tilted toward the termination.

analysis.notes: the integral gamma + ln(2kl) - Ci(2kl) - 1 + sin(2kl)/(2kl), which carries all the length dependence

Rr = 60*[...] to three figures, since eta0/(2*pi) = 59.96. Derived by integrating the travelling-wave pattern and confirmed against quadrature at 0.01, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8 lambda; the l -> 0 limit reproduces the uniform-current dipole's 80*pi^2*(l/lambda)^2 exactly.

Balanis 10-8. The arccos argument is clamped at 0, so a wire shorter than 0.371 lambda returns a broadside maximum - which is the correct short-wire limit, and makes the directivity formula return 1.5 there.
Cone half-angle measured from the wire, toward the terminated end. Accurate to 0.3 deg at 4 lambda and 0.8 deg at 2 lambda; at 1 lambda it is 2.7 deg optimistic.
D = 4*pi*U(theta_max)/Prad in closed form. Using the approximate beam angle instead of the true one costs under 0.1% for l >= 2 lambda.

Indicative only. The termination must match the wire's characteristic impedance against ground (typically 400-600 ohm for a wire well above earth), not the radiation resistance. Half the input power is dissipated there in the ideal travelling-wave case.

validity: l >= 2 lambda for the 0.371 beam-angle approximation to hold within a degree
single pure travelling wave: the termination must actually absorb, or a reflected wave restores the standing-wave pattern and the beam splits
free space. A real long wire runs above earth, which adds an image and tilts the beam upward
the conical beam means the pattern has no single main lobe in a plane, a fact the rhombic and V exist to fix

known_cases.source: Independently reproduced by numerical quadrature of the exact travelling-wave pattern: Rr = 209.551 ohm, true beam maximum at 24.60 deg (the 0.371 fit gives 24.87), D = 9.944 at the true angle and 9.938 at the fitted one.
Quadrature gives Rr = 251.093 ohm and D = 16.994 (12.30 dBi), true beam maximum 17.42 deg against the fitted 17.52.

Limit check, not a design point. A wire far shorter than a wavelength carries an essentially uniform current, so the closed form must approach the infinitesimal dipole: Rr -> 80*pi^2*(l/lambda)^2 = 0.0789568 ohm and D -> 1.5. At 0.01 lambda it gives 0.0788711 ohm (0.11% below the asymptote, as expected of a limit) and 1.5001.

references: Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 10.1-10.2 (eqs. 10-3, 10-8)
Radiation resistance derived here by direct integration and checked against quadrature

archetypes.name: Travelling-wave V antenna
archetypes.summary: Two terminated travelling-wave legs flared from a common feed, angled so their conical beams combine along the axis.

synthesis.notes: Alignment design: each leg makes its own beam-cone angle with the axis, so the two cones meet on the axis. Within a degree of the numerically optimal angle, and worth under 0.3 dB. Clamped at 90 deg for legs shorter than 0.371 lambda.

analysis.notes: apex angle between the legs

Power-law fit to the axial directivity computed from the exact two-leg travelling-wave model at the alignment angle, over 1.5 to 12 lambda. Maximum error 1.3%. NaN outside 1.5-12 lambda: at 0.1 it read a peak directivity of 0.85, below isotropic.
What flaring the line into a V buys over one leg on its own: about 3.5 dB at 4 lambda, because the axial lobe replaces a cone
Indicative. The legs must be terminated in the structure's characteristic impedance to ground; 400-800 ohm is the usual range and it is not derived here.

validity: 1.5 <= l/lambda <= 12, the range the directivity fit was computed over
free space; over ground the pattern tilts and the gain rises by up to 6 dB
both legs terminated, so half the input power goes into the terminations
the fit is for the ALIGNMENT angle; the true optimum is a few degrees tighter and worth about 0.3 dB

known_cases.source: Axial directivity from direct spherical integration of the two-leg travelling-wave model: 22.341 (13.49 dBi) at the 24.87 deg alignment angle; the numerically best angle, 23.63 deg, gives 22.591.
Same model at 2 lambda: 12.128 (10.84 dBi). The axial lobe is confirmed to be the global pattern maximum at the alignment angle for every leg length tested.

references: Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 10.3.1
Directivity computed here from the exact travelling-wave leg model and fitted over 1.5-12 lambda

archetypes.name: Rhombic antenna
archetypes.summary: Four travelling-wave legs in a diamond, terminated at the far apex: a V antenna with its mirror image, for roughly 2.4 dB more.

parameters.name: wire radius
parameters.description: The parameter the spec used to leave out. It sets the termination, and how much power that termination eats, while barely touching the directivity.

synthesis.notes: same alignment rule as the V; the numerical optimum is a few degrees WIDER for the rhombic and worth about 0.3 dB Clamped at 90 deg for legs shorter than 0.371 lambda.

analysis.notes: The idealised four-leg model this spec was built on: an unattenuated travelling wave on every leg and a perfect termination. Kept because the V antenna beside it still uses the same model, so gain_over_v_antenna_db stays like-for-like.

Solved, at the alignment angle and the termination that maximises front-to-back, on a/lambda = 1e-4 wire. The idealised model is 0.24 to 0.45 dB high over leg lengths 2 to 12 lambda: the real current decays as it radiates, which the idealised model ignores. Wire radius moves it only 0.33 dB across 1e-5 to 3e-3 lambda. Fitted in ln(L), worst error 0.33% in D. Solved as built: one closed wire of four legs with the feed at one acute vertex and the resistor as a lumped load at the other (otahub.num.mom.rhombic_model), at 28 segments per wavelength - within about 0.05 dB of converged; 12 per wavelength reads 0.35 dB low. Power into the resistor is accounted for exactly: input = radiated + dissipated to 1e-4. NaN outside 2-12 lambda: at 0.1 it read 0.50, below isotropic.

Like-for-like: both from the idealised travelling-wave model. The V cannot be solved in free space - its terminations need a return path to ground that free space does not have - so comparing a solved rhombic against an idealised V would measure the models, not the antennas.
diamond area - rhombics are large, which is why they were an HF point-to-point antenna and little else

Solved: the resistance that maximises front-to-back, which is the one that best absorbs the forward wave. It is set by the WIRE: 878 ohm at a = 1e-5 lambda, 633 at 1e-4, 387 at 1e-3 - linear in ln(lambda/a) at about 106 ohm per neper, the way a two-wire line's impedance goes. Leg length barely matters (596-635 ohm from 2 to 12 lambda at 1e-4). The flat 600 ohm this spec carried matches the optimum at about a = 1e-4 lambda, typical HF wire, where it is -5%; it is -32% on the thinnest wire and +55% at 1e-3. Worst fit error 0.6%. Solved as built: one closed wire of four legs with the feed at one acute vertex and the resistor as a lumped load at the other (otahub.num.mom.rhombic_model), at 28 segments per wavelength - within about 0.05 dB of converged; 12 per wavelength reads 0.35 dB low. Power into the resistor is accounted for exactly: input = radiated + dissipated to 1e-4.

Fraction of the input power that is radiated rather than burned in the termination: 0.44 at a = 1e-5 lambda, 0.53 at 1e-4, 0.66 at 1e-3. So the old 'about half' holds for thin HF wire and not for fat wire. Worst fit error 0.4%. Solved as built: one closed wire of four legs with the feed at one acute vertex and the resistor as a lumped load at the other (otahub.num.mom.rhombic_model), at 28 segments per wavelength - within about 0.05 dB of converged; 12 per wavelength reads 0.35 dB low. Power into the resistor is accounted for exactly: input = radiated + dissipated to 1e-4.
Directivity less the power the termination absorbs.

validity: 1.5 <= l/lambda <= 12 for the directivity; the solved fit covers 2 to 12
wire radius 1e-5 to 3e-3 wavelengths for the termination and efficiency, which were measured on a 4-wavelength leg and barely depend on length
free space; a real rhombic is horizontal above earth, which adds up to 6 dB and sets the elevation angle
terminated: the termination takes 26% of the input power on fat wire and 56% on the thinnest, so the gain sits 1.3 to 3.5 dB below the directivity
the alignment angle is not the best angle: at 4 lambda the axial directivity peaks near 27 degrees, 0.3 dB above the alignment angle's figure - a wider diamond, not a tighter one
planar rhombic; the alignment angle assumes all four legs are coplanar

known_cases.source: Axial directivity from spherical integration of the exact four-leg model: 39.210 (15.93 dBi). The axial lobe is the global maximum, which is the whole point of the alignment angle. [Now asserted against directivity_travelling_wave_model: this is the idealised model's figure, and directivity_linear is the solved one.]

6 lambda legs give 59.619 (17.75 dBi) against the V's 31.853 (15.03 dBi), a 2.72 dB advantage - both from the same integration [Now asserted against directivity_travelling_wave_model: this is the idealised model's figure, and directivity_linear is the solved one.]
Method of moments, 4-wavelength legs, a/lambda = 1e-4, termination 633 ohm: 15.61 dBi axially, against 15.90 from the idealised travelling-wave model.
Method of moments, 8-wavelength legs, a/lambda = 1e-4, termination 633 ohm: 18.68 dBi axially, against 19.04 from the idealised travelling-wave model.
Method of moments at a/lambda = 0.0001, 4-wavelength legs: front-to-back peaks at 633 ohm, where 53.1% of the input is radiated and the rest burned in the termination.
Method of moments at a/lambda = 0.001, 4-wavelength legs: front-to-back peaks at 387 ohm, where 65.7% of the input is radiated and the rest burned in the termination.

references: Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 10.3.2
Bruce, Beck & Lowry, Horizontal rhombic antennas, Proc. IRE 23(1), 1935
Directivity computed here from the exact four-leg travelling-wave model
Directivity, optimal termination and efficiency solved here by method of moments with the terminating resistor as a lumped load

archetypes.name: Uniform leaky-wave line source
archetypes.summary: Slitted waveguide radiating a fast wave: the beam angle is set by the guide dispersion, so the antenna scans with frequency.

parameters.name: normalised leakage
parameters.description: alpha/k0; set by how far the slit is opened

analysis.notes: TE10 dispersion. Always below 1, so the guided wave is FAST and therefore radiates once the guide is opened - this is the whole mechanism.

sin(theta) = beta/k0, measured from broadside. Approaches endfire well above cutoff and swings toward broadside as the guide nears cutoff - but never reaches it, which is the classic leaky-wave broadside blind spot. That is the array factor's peak. The slit's own element pattern (cos theta in power along the scan plane) pulls the pattern's peak toward broadside: 0.5 degrees at the default, 0.1-1 degree on long sources, up to 4 near endfire on short ones.
the same beam measured from the guide axis
alpha L in nepers: the leakage accumulated along the source. 1.13 at the default, which radiates 90% of the power before the load.

Half-power beamwidth in the scan plane: k(alpha L) lambda/(L cos theta). The aperture is not uniform - the wave leaks away along it, amplitude exp(-alpha x) - so k is the exponential aperture's own half-power width, solved exactly and tabulated in alpha L: 0.886 (the uniform aperture's 0.88 this spec carried) as alpha L goes to 0, 0.922 at the default 1.13, 1.14 at 3. Checked against the pattern of the line source integrated directly (element pattern included): within 2.2% from broadside to about a beamwidth short of endfire; closer to endfire the 1/cos(theta) widening overstates it, by up to 21% for a 5-wavelength source with beta/k0 = 0.85.
Power actually radiated before the wave reaches the load. alpha*L = 1.15 gives 90%, the usual design target; the remainder is burnt in the termination.

SOLVED: 4L/lambda times the exponential aperture's taper efficiency (2/(alpha L)) tanh(alpha L/2), with a small fitted correction in 1/L - the directivity of a leaky line source in a ground plane radiating into the half space above it (an x-directed magnetic line current exp(-(alpha + j beta) x), its element pattern included). Fitted to direct integration of that source over beta/k0 0.3-0.85, L 5-40 wavelengths and alpha L 0.3-3: 3.5% worst on 80 designs, 1.1% on 10 held out; without the correction it reads up to 11% low on short sources. It does NOT fall as the beam scans: the beam narrows in the scan plane but opens round the guide's axis, and a line source's directivity holds (15.7 dBi at 37, 49 and 57 degrees at the default). This spec had 2(L/lambda) cos(theta) (1 - exp(-2 alpha L)): the free-space line source's 2L/lambda, a planar aperture's cos(theta) that a line source does not have, and the power lost to the load, which belongs in the gain - 10.7 dBi at the default where the source has 15.7. A slit in a bare guide, with no ground plane, radiates round the guide too and sits up to 3 dB lower (12.7 dBi for an isotropic cross-section).
Directivity times the fraction of the power radiated before the load (a lossless guide otherwise): what the old 'directivity' entry was reaching for. 15.2 dBi at the default.

validity: uniform (non-periodic) leakage, so only the forward quadrant is scanned; a periodic structure scans through broadside using the n = -1 harmonic
beam angle assumes the leakage is weak enough not to perturb beta, true for alpha/k0 below about 0.05
no beam squint correction for the slit's own reactance
the guide must be above cutoff: below it the wave is evanescent and nothing radiates
directivity, gain and beamwidth are for the slit in a ground plane, radiating into the half space; a slit in a bare guide sits up to 3 dB lower in directivity
directivity fitted over beta/k0 0.3-0.85, L 5-40 wavelengths and alpha L 0.3-3 (3.5% worst); the beamwidth formula needs the beam at least a beamwidth from endfire

known_cases.source: WR-90 at 10 GHz: cutoff 6.557 GHz, guide wavelength 39.71 mm against a free-space 29.98 mm, so sin(theta) = 0.7549 and the beam sits 49.0 deg from broadside. Cross-checked against this toolkit's own rectangular-waveguide module.
Same guide at the bottom of the X band: the beam has swung 12 deg toward broadside. Across 8.2-12.4 GHz the beam scans 36.9 to 58.1 deg - frequency scanning, with no phase shifters.
Top of the X band, completing the scan range
